props.title: Ever After
props.initialSlug: A Cinderella tale where brains trump magic

sections.content: Ever After brilliantly reimagines Cinderella as a Renaissance-era feminist tale, with Drew Barrymore's headstrong Danielle defying fairy tale conventions. Unlike Disney's Cinderella (1950), this version grounds the story in historical reality - no magic pumpkins or fairy godmothers needed. Instead, it draws inspiration from actual Renaissance figures like Leonardo da Vinci (played by Patrick Godfrey) and weaves in themes of class struggle, female education, and self-determination that feel startlingly modern. The film helped launch a wave of fairy tale retellings like The Brothers Grimm (2005) and Mirror Mirror (2012).

sections.content: The film's costume design by Jenny Beavan deserves special attention, earning an Academy Award nomination for its historically-inspired yet imaginative Renaissance wardrobe. This attention to period detail influenced later fairy tale adaptations like Snow White and the Huntsman (2012) and Maleficent (2014), which similarly aimed to ground magical stories in tangible historical settings. The "breathing" paintings and innovative glass slippers particularly showcase how practical effects can enhance fairy tale elements without relying on CGI.

What sets Ever After apart is its framing device - starting with the Brothers Grimm visiting Danielle's descendant to learn the "true" story. This clever structure, later echoed in films like Enchanted (2007) and Into the Woods (2014), allows the film to both honor and challenge fairy tale traditions. The movie's emphasis on books, learning, and intellectual curiosity was groundbreaking for the genre, influencing later "bookish" heroines like Belle in Beauty and the Beast (2017). sections.content: Ever After revolutionized how fairy tale romances could be portrayed on screen. Instead of love at first sight, Danielle and Prince Henry's relationship develops through philosophical debates and shared adventures. This more complex approach to fairy tale romance influenced films like Frozen (2013) and Brave (2012), which similarly questioned traditional "prince charming" narratives. The film's handling of class issues and servants' rights was notably progressive for its time, predating similar themes in Downton Abbey (2019) and The Favourite (2018).
